csharp: By default, what does the C# compiler (Roslyn) emit into a .dll assembly?
IL (CIL) code that the JIT compiles at run time
Native x86 machine code ready to execute
Java bytecode for a JVM to interpret
Plain source text parsed on every launch
C# compiles to Common Intermediate Language plus metadata; the CLR's JIT compiler turns IL into native code when methods are first called (ahead-of-time options exist but are not the default).
In .NET, from what object size are allocations placed on the Large Object Heap by default?
85,000 bytes or larger
1 MB or larger
4,096 bytes or larger
65,536 bytes or larger
Objects of 85,000 bytes or more go to the LOH, which is collected with generation 2 and is not compacted by default, so frequent large allocations can cause fragmentation.
What happens when a C# async method reaches await on a Task that has not completed yet?
It returns to its caller and resumes when the task completes
It blocks the current thread until the task completes
It starts a new thread and moves the method onto it
It throws InvalidOperationException immediately
await on an incomplete task registers a continuation and returns control to the caller; no thread is blocked while waiting.
Why is async void discouraged in C# except for event handlers?
Callers cannot await it or catch its exceptions
It forces the method to run synchronously on the UI thread
It cannot contain more than one await expression
It is compiled into a blocking Thread.Sleep call
An async void method gives the caller no Task to await, and an exception thrown inside it is raised on the SynchronizationContext, where it usually crashes the process.
In a WinForms or classic ASP.NET app, the UI thread calls GetDataAsync().Result, and GetDataAsync awaits without ConfigureAwait(false). What typically happens?
A deadlock: the continuation waits for the blocked UI thread
A compile error, because Result is not allowed on Task<T>
The call silently moves to a background thread and succeeds
The compiler rewrites the Result call into an await
The continuation is posted back to the UI SynchronizationContext, but that thread is blocked on .Result, so neither can proceed. Use await all the way up instead.
In C#: var nums = new List<int> { 1, 2 }; var q = nums.Where(n => n > 0); nums.Add(3); What does q.Count() return?
LINQ queries use deferred execution: Where only runs when q is enumerated by Count(), which happens after 3 was added.
What does new[] { 1, 2, 3, 4 }.Where(x => x % 2 == 0).Select(x => x * 10).Sum() return in C#?
Where keeps 2 and 4, Select turns them into 20 and 40, and Sum adds them to 60.
What is the most a single C# class can inherit from or implement?
One base class plus any number of interfaces
Two base classes plus any number of interfaces
Any number of base classes but one interface
One base class and at most one interface
C# allows single class inheritance but multiple interface implementation, so a class can extend one abstract class and implement many interfaces.
What is the main restriction the event keyword adds compared with a public delegate field in C#?
Outside code can only subscribe or unsubscribe, not invoke it
Outside code can invoke it but cannot subscribe to it
It can hold only one handler at a time, unlike a delegate field
Its handlers must be static methods declared in the same class
An event exposes only += and -= to other classes; only the declaring class can raise it or replace the handler list.
In C#: Action<int> a = x => Console.Write(x); a += x => Console.Write(x * 2); a(5); What is printed?
Delegates are multicast: += adds a second handler, and invoking a runs both in order, printing 5 and then 10.
What does the constraint where T : new() require in a C# generic method?
T must have a public parameterless constructor
T must be a reference type created with new
T must be a type declared in the same assembly
T must implement an interface named INew
The new() constraint lets the generic code write new T(), so the type argument must expose a public parameterless constructor.
Why can IEnumerable<string> be assigned to IEnumerable<object> in C#, while List<string> cannot be assigned to List<object>?
IEnumerable<T> declares T as covariant (out T)
List<T> is sealed, which blocks all conversions
string is a value type that boxes to object
IEnumerable<T> is not really a generic interface
IEnumerable<out T> only returns T, so covariance is safe. List<T> also accepts T in Add, so it is invariant; allowing the conversion would let you add a non-string.
In C#, given record Point(int X, int Y); var a = new Point(1, 2); var b = new Point(1, 2); What does a == b return?
true
false
A compile error
Hash-dependent
Records get compiler-generated value equality, so two instances with equal property values compare equal with ==, unlike ordinary classes.
In C#, a struct type has a mutable field X. After var b = a; b.X = 5; what is true about a.X?
It is unchanged, because b is a copy of a
It is 5, because a and b share one object
The code fails, because structs are immutable
The code fails, because structs cannot be copied
Structs are value types, so assignment copies the whole value; changing b does not affect a. A class instance would be shared instead.
In ASP.NET Core dependency injection, which service lifetime creates one instance per HTTP request?
Scoped
Singleton
Transient
Pooled
Scoped services live for one scope, and ASP.NET Core creates a scope per request. Transient creates a new instance every time it is resolved.
In ASP.NET Core, what goes wrong when a singleton service takes a scoped service such as a DbContext in its constructor?
The scoped instance is captured and outlives its scope
The scoped service is recreated on every method call
The singleton is rebuilt once per HTTP request
The container turns the singleton into a transient
This is a captive dependency: the singleton keeps the first scoped instance forever, which is unsafe for DbContext. Scope validation in Development throws an error for it.
With nullable reference types enabled in C#, what does string? name declare?
A string that may be null, tracked by compiler warnings
A Nullable<string> struct wrapping the value
A string that throws at run time when set to null
A string that defaults to empty instead of null
For reference types, ? is a compile-time annotation: the compiler warns about unsafe dereferences. Nothing changes at run time, and Nullable<T> applies only to value types.
Which C# expression gets the System.Type object for a class named Order without needing an instance?
typeof(Order)
Order.GetType()
nameof(Order)
Type.Of<Order>()
typeof is evaluated at compile time for a type name. GetType() is an instance method, and nameof returns only the string "Order".
What does a C# using statement such as using (var f = File.OpenRead(path)) { ... } guarantee?
f.Dispose() is called when the block exits, even on exceptions
f is garbage collected right after the block ends, freeing memory
f is reopened automatically if an exception occurs in the block
f can be shared safely across several threads inside the block
using compiles to try/finally that calls Dispose, so the file handle is released deterministically. Memory is still reclaimed later by the GC.
In the .NET dispose pattern, why does Dispose() call GC.SuppressFinalize(this)?
Cleanup is already done, so the finalizer need not run
It forces an immediate garbage collection of the object
It prevents Dispose from being called a second time
It frees the managed memory of the object
Objects with finalizers survive an extra GC and go through the finalization queue. After explicit cleanup, SuppressFinalize removes that cost.
java: What does javac produce from a .java source file?
.class files containing JVM bytecode
Native executables for the host OS
.jar files containing C++ object code
Script files run by the JRE shell
javac compiles source to platform-independent bytecode in .class files, which any JVM can load and run. A .jar is just an archive of such files.
Which JVM component turns frequently executed bytecode into native machine code at run time?
The JIT compiler
The class loader
The bytecode verifier
The garbage collector
HotSpot first interprets bytecode, then the Just-In-Time compiler compiles hot methods to native code. The class loader only loads and links classes.
Which garbage collector does the HotSpot JVM use by default on server-class machines since Java 9?
G1 (Garbage-First)
Serial (single-threaded)
Parallel (throughput)
CMS (Concurrent Mark Sweep)
JEP 248 made G1 the default in Java 9. Parallel was the previous default, and CMS was later removed in Java 14.
What is the main design goal of ZGC in modern Java (JDK 15 and later)?
Very short pauses that do not grow with heap size
Maximum throughput with long stop-the-world pauses
Minimal memory use on single-core devices
Reference counting to free objects instantly
ZGC does most of its work concurrently with the application, keeping pauses in the millisecond range even for very large heaps.
What does the volatile keyword guarantee for a Java field?
A write by one thread is visible to later reads by others
Compound actions like count++ on it become atomic
Only one thread at a time can access the field
The field is kept in a CPU register for speed
volatile gives visibility and ordering (happens-before) but not atomicity of read-modify-write. count++ on a volatile int can still lose updates.
Two Java threads each run count++ 1000 times on a shared int field with no synchronization. What is the final value of count?
It may be less than 2000, because count++ is not atomic
Exactly 2000, because int writes are atomic
Exactly 1000, because the threads overwrite each other
A compile error, because the field is not volatile
count++ is read, add, write; interleaved threads can overwrite each other's updates. Use AtomicInteger or synchronized to get exactly 2000.
A ThreadPoolExecutor has corePoolSize 2, maximumPoolSize 4 and an unbounded LinkedBlockingQueue. How many worker threads run under heavy load?
2, because extra tasks wait in the unbounded queue
4, because the pool grows to its maximum when busy
Unlimited, because the queue has no capacity limit
1, because only one thread polls the queue
New threads beyond the core size are created only when the queue rejects a task. An unbounded queue never fills, so maximumPoolSize has no effect.
Because of type erasure, what does new ArrayList<String>().getClass() == new ArrayList<Integer>().getClass() evaluate to in Java?
true
false
A compile error
An exception
Generic type arguments are erased at compile time, so both objects have the same runtime class, java.util.ArrayList.
Which Java method signature accepts both a List<Integer> and a List<Double> and lets you read elements as Number?
void sum(List<? extends Number> list)
void sum(List<Number> list)
void sum(List<? super Number> list)
void sum(List<Object> list)
Generics are invariant, so List<Integer> is not a List<Number>. An upper-bounded wildcard accepts any list of Number subtypes for reading ("producer extends").
In the Spring Framework, what does @Autowired on a constructor do?
Asks the container to inject matching beans as arguments
Marks the class as a REST controller
Opens a new database connection on each call
Makes the constructor run on a background thread
Spring resolves each constructor parameter from the beans in the application context. Since Spring 4.3 a single constructor is autowired even without the annotation.
What is the default scope of a bean in the Spring Framework?
Singleton: one shared instance per container
Prototype: a new instance on every lookup
Request: one instance per HTTP request
Session: one instance per HTTP session
Unless another scope is declared, Spring creates one instance per application context and injects that same instance everywhere.
What does List.of(1, 2, 3, 4).stream().filter(x -> x > 1).map(x -> x * 2).toList() return in Java 16 or later?
filter keeps 2, 3 and 4, then map doubles them. Stream.toList() was added in Java 16 and returns an unmodifiable list.
What does Stream.of(1, 2, 3).peek(System.out::print).map(x -> x * 2); print in Java if no terminal operation follows?
Nothing is printed
It prints 123
It prints 246
It prints 123 then 246
Intermediate operations are lazy; the pipeline runs only when a terminal operation such as forEach or toList is called.
Why does int n = 0; Runnable r = () -> n++; fail to compile in Java?
Lambdas can capture only effectively final local variables
Runnable lambdas cannot read any local variables at all
The ++ operator is not allowed inside any lambda expression body
Runnable lambdas must return an int value to the caller
A lambda may read captured locals only if they are never reassigned. n++ modifies n, so the compiler rejects it.
Which standard Java collection gives key lookups with the keys kept in sorted order?
TreeMap
HashMap
LinkedHashMap
Hashtable
TreeMap is a red-black tree with O(log n) operations and sorted keys. LinkedHashMap keeps insertion order, not sorted order.
A Java class overrides equals() but not hashCode(). What problem appears when its objects are used as HashMap keys?
Equal keys may land in different buckets, so lookups fail
The code fails to compile when such a class is used as a HashMap key
Every key is placed into the same bucket, so lookups slow down
The map sorts its keys using equals() instead of hashCode()
HashMap finds the bucket by hashCode() first. Equal objects with different identity hash codes end up in different buckets, so get() can return null.
In Java: class A { void f() { System.out.print("A"); } } class B extends A { void f() { System.out.print("B"); } } What does A a = new B(); a.f(); print?
B
A
AB
BA
Instance methods are dispatched on the runtime type of the object (dynamic dispatch), so B's override runs even through an A reference.
In Java, class A has static void f() printing "A", and subclass B declares static void f() printing "B". What does A a = new B(); a.f(); print?
A
B
AB
BA
Static methods are not overridden but hidden, and calls are bound by the declared type of the reference, so A.f() runs. The compiler only warns about calling it through an instance.
Which kind of Java exception must be either caught or declared with throws?
Checked exceptions such as IOException
Unchecked ones such as NullPointerException
Errors such as OutOfMemoryError
Any subclass of RuntimeException
The compiler enforces handling only for checked exceptions: Exception subclasses outside RuntimeException. RuntimeException and Error are unchecked.
What does this Java method return: int f() { try { return 1; } finally { return 2; } }
Nothing
An exception
The finally block runs after the try's return value is computed, and its own return replaces that value. Returning from finally is legal but discouraged.
kotlin: In Kotlin, what is the value of name?.length ?: 0 when name is null?
null
An exception
The safe call ?. yields null instead of throwing, and the Elvis operator ?: then substitutes 0.
What does the !! operator do in Kotlin, as in name!!.length?
Throws a NullPointerException if name is null
Returns 0 instead of failing if name is null
Skips the call and returns null if name is null
Marks name as nullable only for that call
!! asserts that the value is not null and converts it to a non-null type; if it is null, a NullPointerException is thrown.
Which kotlinx.coroutines dispatcher is intended for blocking I/O such as file or network calls?
Dispatchers.IO
Dispatchers.Main
Dispatchers.Default
Dispatchers.Unconfined
Dispatchers.IO uses a larger, elastic thread pool for blocking calls. Dispatchers.Default is sized to CPU cores and meant for CPU-bound work.
What is the key difference between launch and async in kotlinx.coroutines?
async returns a Deferred whose result you get with await()
launch returns a Deferred whose value you read with await()
async blocks the calling thread until it finishes
launch can start coroutines only on Dispatchers.Main
launch returns a Job and is used for fire-and-forget work, while async returns Deferred<T>, a Job with a result.
In Kotlin: coroutineScope { launch { error("x") }; launch { delay(5000) } }. What happens to the second child when the first one throws?
It is cancelled, and the exception propagates from coroutineScope
It keeps running for the full 5 seconds, and then the scope ends normally
It restarts automatically with a fresh Job after the failure
It is promoted to replace the failed coroutine in the scope
Structured concurrency: a failing child cancels its parent scope, which cancels all other children, and coroutineScope rethrows the exception. supervisorScope behaves differently.
In Kotlin, given data class User(val name: String, val age: Int), what does User("A", 1) == User("A", 1) return?
true
false
A compile error
Identity-based
Data classes generate equals() and hashCode() from the primary constructor properties, and == calls equals().
Which member does a Kotlin data class NOT generate automatically from its primary constructor properties?
compareTo()
copy()
component1()
toString()
Data classes get equals, hashCode, toString, copy and componentN functions. Ordering is not generated; you must implement Comparable yourself.
In Kotlin, after declaring fun String.shout() = uppercase() + "!", which call works and what does it return?
"hi".shout(), returning "HI!"
shout("hi"), returning "HI!"
"hi".shout, returning "HI!"
String.shout("hi"), returning "HI!"
An extension function is called like a member on a receiver of that type, and inside it this refers to the receiver string.
In Kotlin: open class A; class B : A(); fun A.name() = "A"; fun B.name() = "B"; val x: A = B(). What does x.name() return?
"AB"
A compile error
Extension functions are resolved statically by the declared type of the expression, here A, not by the runtime type.
Why can a Kotlin when expression on a value of a sealed class type omit the else branch?
The compiler knows every subclass and checks exhaustiveness
when returns null by default whenever no branch matches the value
A sealed class is limited to exactly two subclasses
else is added implicitly and throws at run time
All direct subclasses of a sealed class are known at compile time, so the compiler can verify that every case is covered.
Since Kotlin 1.5, where can the direct subclasses of a sealed class be declared?
In the same module and package as the sealed class
In any module that depends on the sealed class
Only inside the body of the sealed class itself
Only in Java files in the same project
Kotlin 1.5 relaxed the rule from the same file to the same module and package, which still keeps the set of subclasses closed.
What does marking a higher-order function as inline do in Kotlin?
Copies its body and lambda arguments into each call site
Runs the function on a separate background thread
Caches its result for repeated calls with same args
Forces lambda arguments to be stored as objects
Inlining removes the cost of allocating function objects for lambdas and also enables non-local returns from those lambdas.
Which Kotlin feature can be used only in an inline function?
A reified type parameter, as in <reified T>
A vararg parameter, as in vararg x: Int
A default argument, as in x: Int = 0
A nullable return type, as in : Int?
Generic types are erased on the JVM; reified works because the inlined body is copied with the actual type, so checks like x is T are possible.
In Kotlin, class Car declares fun create() inside its companion object. How do you call it from Kotlin code?
Car.create()
Car().create()
Car.companion.create()
new Car.create()
Companion object members are called through the class name. Car.Companion.create() also works, but lowercase companion does not.
Which annotation makes a Kotlin companion object function callable from Java as a real static method, Car.create()?
@JvmStatic
@JvmField
@JvmOverloads
@JvmName
Without @JvmStatic, Java must call Car.Companion.create(). @JvmField exposes properties as fields, and @JvmOverloads generates overloads for default arguments.
A Java method with no nullability annotations returns String. How does Kotlin see this return type?
As a platform type, String!, that may be used as either
As String?, so every use needs a null check
As String, guaranteed non-null by the compiler
As Any, because Java types are erased
Platform types relax null checks for Java values; you choose nullable or non-null, and a wrong guess can still fail at run time.
What happens when a cold Kotlin Flow is built with flow { emit(1) } but collect is never called on it?
The block does not run and nothing is emitted
It emits 1 immediately into an internal buffer
It throws because no collector has been attached
It runs once on Dispatchers.Default in the background
Flows built with flow { } are cold: the block runs anew for each collector, and only when collection starts.
Which statement about StateFlow in kotlinx.coroutines is true?
It holds a current value and gives it to each new collector
It has no value until the first emit call happens
It replays every past value to each new collector
It is cold and restarts its producer per collector
StateFlow needs an initial value, keeps only the latest value, and is a hot SharedFlow with replay 1 that skips equal consecutive values.
What does listOf(1, 2, 3).fold(10) { acc, x -> acc + x } return in Kotlin?
fold starts with the initial accumulator 10 and adds each element: 10 + 1 + 2 + 3 = 16.
Which is the correct Kotlin type for a function value that takes two Ints and returns an Int?
(Int, Int) -> Int
Function<Int, Int, Int>
(Int, Int) => Int
fun(Int, Int): Int
Kotlin function types use parentheses for parameters and -> for the return type. => is Scala or JavaScript syntax.
swift: Two Swift class instances hold strong references to each other, and nothing else references them. What happens under ARC?
Neither is deallocated, so their memory leaks
ARC detects the cycle and frees both of them
The older object is freed first, then the other
The app crashes at the next assignment
ARC only counts references and has no cycle collector, so each object keeps the other's count above zero. Break cycles with weak or unowned.
In a Swift delegate pattern, how should the child object usually declare its delegate property to avoid a retain cycle?
weak var delegate: MyDelegate?
strong var delegate: MyDelegate?
lazy var delegate: MyDelegate?
static var delegate: MyDelegate?
weak does not keep the delegate alive and becomes nil when it is freed. The protocol must be class-bound (AnyObject) for weak to be allowed.
When is unowned preferred over weak for a reference in Swift?
When the referenced object is sure to outlive the reference
When the reference should become nil automatically after deallocation
When the referenced type is a struct, not a class
When the reference must keep its object alive for its lifetime
unowned is non-optional and does not become nil; accessing it after the object is freed traps. Use it only when the lifetime guarantee holds.
Which capture list stops a stored Swift closure from strongly retaining self?
[weak self]
[strong self]
[inout self]
[copy self]
[weak self] captures self weakly as an optional, breaking the cycle when self also stores the closure. [unowned self] is the other valid choice.
What does a protocol extension let you do in Swift?
Give default method implementations to conforming types
Add stored properties to every conforming type
Make a protocol inherit from a concrete class
Make a struct conform to a protocol dynamically at run time
Protocol extensions add methods and computed properties with bodies, which every conforming type gets unless it provides its own.
In Swift: protocol P {}; extension P { func hi() -> String { "P" } }; struct S: P { func hi() -> String { "S" } }; let x: P = S(). What does x.hi() return?
"PS"
A compile error
hi() is not a requirement declared in P, so a call through the P type uses static dispatch to the extension method. Declaring hi() in P would make it return "S".
What does if let name = user.name { print(name) } do in Swift?
Prints name only when user.name is not nil
Crashes at run time when user.name is nil
Prints the word nil when user.name is nil
Prints name with an Optional(...) wrapper
Optional binding unwraps the value into a non-optional constant and runs the block only if the optional holds a value.
In Swift: let a: Int? = nil; let b = a ?? 5. What is b?
5, of type Int
nil, of type Int?
Optional(5), of type Int?
0, of type Int
The nil-coalescing operator returns the unwrapped value or the default; with a non-optional default, the result type is Int.
What must the else branch of a Swift guard let statement do?
Exit the current scope, for example with return or throw
Assign a default value to the guarded variable and continue
Force-unwrap the optional with the ! operator
Fall through into the code that follows the guard statement
The compiler requires guard's else to leave the scope (return, throw, break, continue or a Never call), so the unwrapped value is safe afterward.
In Swift: struct P { var x = 1 }; var a = P(); var b = a; b.x = 2. What is a.x?
nil
Structs are value types: var b = a copies the value, so changing b does not change a. With a class, a.x would be 2.
Why must a Swift struct method that changes a stored property be marked mutating?
self is immutable inside struct methods by default
Structs live on the heap, so writes need locking
mutating makes the method run on the main thread
mutating lets subclasses override the method
Struct methods get self as an immutable value; mutating lets the method modify self, which works only on var instances.
What does a Swift actor guarantee about its mutable state?
Only one task at a time can access it
It is copied into every task that reads it
It is stored in thread-local storage
It can be read only from the main thread
An actor serializes access to its isolated state, which prevents data races. Code outside must use await to reach it.
Why do you write await when calling an actor's method from outside the actor in Swift?
The call may suspend until the actor is free to run it
Actor methods are compiled as throwing functions
await converts the result into an optional value
await blocks the caller's thread until the actor method returns
Crossing into actor isolation is a potential suspension point; the caller's task suspends without blocking its thread.
What does async let x = fetchA() do in Swift?
Starts fetchA as a child task that runs concurrently
Calls fetchA and blocks until its value is ready
Declares x as a variable that can be reassigned
Runs fetchA on the main actor after the scope ends
async let starts the work right away in parallel with the following code; you get the value later with await x.
What does [3, 1, 2].sorted { $0 > $1 } return in Swift?
The trailing closure is the ordering predicate; $0 > $1 places larger elements first, giving descending order.
When must a closure parameter be marked @escaping in Swift?
When it is stored or called after the function returns
When it can throw an error during the call
When it captures no variables from outer scope
When it is called more than once inside the function body
Closure parameters are non-escaping by default. Storing one in a property or calling it asynchronously later needs @escaping.
In SwiftUI, which property wrapper declares simple local state owned by a view, such as a Bool for a toggle?
@State
@Binding
@Environment
@Published
@State storage is owned by SwiftUI for that view, and changing it re-renders the body. @Binding refers to state owned elsewhere.
In SwiftUI, what is a @Binding property in a child view used for?
Reading and writing state owned by a parent view
Storing state that survives app restarts
Declaring state that the child creates and owns
Observing posts from NotificationCenter
A Binding is a two-way reference to a source of truth elsewhere, usually passed in from a parent's @State with the $ prefix.
What does try? do when the called Swift function throws an error?
Returns nil instead of propagating the error
Crashes the app with the error's message
Retries the call once before giving up
Returns the error converted to a String
try? converts the result into an optional and discards the error. try! is the variant that crashes when an error is thrown.
What must a type marked with @propertyWrapper provide in Swift?
A wrappedValue property
A projectedValue property
An init(from: Decoder) initializer
A static shared instance
wrappedValue is the only requirement; it is what the wrapped property reads and writes. projectedValue is optional and is exposed with $.
objective-c: What does ARC (Automatic Reference Counting) do in Objective-C?
Inserts retain and release calls at compile time
Runs a tracing garbage collector at run time
Frees all objects when the app enters background
Detects and breaks retain cycles automatically
ARC is a compiler feature: it adds the memory management calls you wrote by hand under MRC. It does not collect cycles.
Under ARC, what happens to a __weak Objective-C reference when its object is deallocated?
It is set to nil automatically
It keeps pointing at the freed memory
It retains the object to keep it alive
It raises an exception on the next access
Zeroing weak references become nil on deallocation. __unsafe_unretained is the variant that keeps a dangling pointer.
Under manual retain-release (MRC), what does a retain property setter typically do?
Retains the new value and releases the old one
Copies the new value and retains the old one as a backup
Releases the new value and keeps the old one
Assigns the new value with no memory calls
A retain setter takes ownership of the incoming object and gives up ownership of the previous one, taking care when both are the same object.
What does declaring a variable with the type id mean in Objective-C?
It can point to any Objective-C object
It holds an integer object identifier
It is a constant that cannot be reassigned
It can hold only NSObject subclasses
id is a generic object pointer; the compiler allows any message to be sent to it, and the runtime resolves it.
What does the Objective-C compiler turn a message send like [obj doSomething:42] into?
A call to objc_msgSend with obj, the selector and 42
A direct C function call that is resolved at link time
A vtable lookup fixed at compile time
A performSelector call on the main thread
Every message is dispatched at run time by objc_msgSend, which finds the method implementation for the selector in the receiver's class.
What is a SEL in Objective-C?
The runtime identifier for a method name
A pointer to a method's compiled code in the class
A reference to an object's class
A block that wraps a method call
A selector names a method, as in @selector(doSomething:). The pointer to the compiled function is a separate type, IMP.
By default, what happens when an Objective-C object receives a message it does not implement and has no forwarding set up?
An unrecognized selector exception is raised
The call quietly returns 0 or nil to the sender
The runtime adds an empty method for it and continues
The superclass's init method is called
After resolution and forwarding fail, doesNotRecognizeSelector: raises NSInvalidArgumentException ("unrecognized selector sent to instance").
What can an Objective-C category add to an existing class such as NSString?
New methods, without needing its source code
New instance variables stored in each object
A new superclass for the existing class
Synthesized properties backed by new ivars
Categories add methods, even to framework classes. They cannot add ivars, so a property declared in a category gets no storage.
Two categories on the same Objective-C class both define a method with the same name. What happens?
Which version is used at run time is undefined
The compiler merges both bodies into one
Both run, in alphabetical order of file name
The linker refuses to build the app
Apple's documentation warns that the runtime picks one implementation in an undefined way, which is why category methods on shared classes use prefixes.
In Objective-C: int x = 1; void (^b)(void) = ^{ NSLog(@"%d", x); }; x = 2; b(); What is logged?
A block captures local variables by value when it is created, so later changes to x are not seen. Declaring x with __block would print 2.
Why do Objective-C developers write __weak typeof(self) weakSelf = self; before creating a block that self stores?
To avoid a retain cycle between self and the block
To make the block run faster on the main thread
To let the block change self's class dynamically at run time
To give the block a copied snapshot of self
A block retains objects it captures. If self also owns the block, capturing self strongly creates a cycle that ARC cannot free.
Why is a delegate property in Objective-C usually declared weak?
The delegate often owns the object, so strong makes a cycle
Weak properties are faster to read than strong ones
Protocol-typed properties cannot be declared strong
Weak makes all of the delegate methods optional to implement
A view controller typically owns a table view and is also its delegate; a strong back reference would keep both alive forever.
How do you safely call an @optional protocol method on an Objective-C delegate?
Check respondsToSelector: before sending the message
Check isKindOfClass: before sending the message
Check conformsToProtocol: before sending it
Wrap the call in @try and ignore the exception
Conforming to the protocol does not mean an optional method is implemented, so test the specific selector first.
Why is copy usually preferred over strong for an NSString property in Objective-C?
A mutable string passed in cannot change it later
copy makes the property thread-safe for writes
strong is not allowed on object properties
copy keeps the string in a faster memory area
If an NSMutableString is assigned to a strong property, later mutations show through. copy stores an immutable snapshot (cheap for an immutable string).
What does the default atomic attribute on an Objective-C property guarantee?
Each get or set is whole, but the object is not fully thread-safe
Every operation on the owning object becomes thread-safe
The property is kept in a CPU register for speed
The property cannot be changed after init returns
atomic ensures a getter never returns a half-written value. It does not make sequences of calls or the object's other state thread-safe, and it costs some speed.

nil is converted to NSNull and then released by the array
addObject: is a plain C function, so nil is dereferenced

NSObject
[NSNull null] returns a singleton that represents "no value" inside collections, which cannot hold nil.

a == b && a != nil

== compares pointers, not contents. compare: returns NSComparisonResult, where equality is NSOrderedSame (0), not YES.

An immutable NSArray of two NSNumber objects

An NSSet containing two NSNumber objects

A trait cannot declare any concrete methods
A class can extend many classes but one trait
A trait cannot contain fields with values
Scala keeps single class inheritance but allows many traits with with, and traits can hold concrete methods and fields.

Sends the message and returns at once, with no reply
Sends the message and waits for the actor's reply
Creates a new actor named Greet on that reference
Stops the actor after it has processed Greet

So its internal state needs no locks
So messages can be sent only from the main thread
So the JVM can skip garbage collection for it
So every message gets its own new thread
Because only one message is handled at a time, the actor's private state is never accessed concurrently, avoiding locks and data races.

When the enclosing class is loaded
